summary: Specifies PNG, an extensible file format for lossless, portable, well-compressed storage of raster images. It was meant as a patent-free replacement for GIF. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: PNG is a file format for images that never loses picture detail. RFC 2083 defines how a PNG file is put together: a short signature, then a series of chunks, each with a type name, a length and a check number that catches damage in transit. Optional chunks add colour information, transparency and text.

questions: what is the difference between png and gif
subtitle: A chunked image format for lossless, portable storage of raster images, designed to replace GIF.

tldr.problem: GIF was no longer freely usable, and no other common image format could replace it while keeping what GIF did well, such as streaming and progressive display.
tldr.mechanism: PNG stores an image as a fixed signature followed by typed chunks: an image header, an optional palette, compressed image data and a trailer. Every chunk carries a CRC, and extra chunks hold transparency, gamma and text information.
tldr.outcome: The specification defines the media type image/png and a format that decoders can extend safely without breaking older ones. RFC 2083 itself is Historic, so it is no longer a current standards document.

today: RFC 2083 is Historic, so it is no longer a current standards document, and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it. It was published in March 1997 as an Informational specification that defines the media type image/png.

sections.title: Goals and Design Principles
sections.content:
RFC 2083 specifies PNG, an extensible file format for the lossless, portable, well-compressed storage of raster images. The authors describe it as a legally unencumbered, well-specified standard for lossless bitmapped image files, and they pronounce it as the word ping.

The initial motivation was to replace GIF. PNG keeps what GIF did well: indexed-color images of up to 256 colours, streamability so a file can be read and written serially, progressive display, transparency, ancillary information such as comments, complete hardware and platform independence, and effective lossless compression.

What PNG adds is truecolor images of up to 48 bits per pixel, grayscale images of up to 16 bits per pixel, a full alpha channel, gamma information so that images display at the right brightness on different equipment, and straightforward detection of file corruption. The RFC also sets out the qualities the format is designed to have: simple and portable to implement, legally unencumbered, well compressed, interchangeable (any conforming decoder must read all conforming files), flexible enough for future extensions, and robust. In this specification the word must indicates a mandatory requirement and should indicates recommended behaviour.

The rationale appendix explains the choice of a new format. GIF was no longer freely usable and no other commonly used format could directly replace it, and adapting an existing format with a different compression scheme would have required new code anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors wanted a lossless image format that anyone could implement without licence problems, and that would keep the useful parts of GIF while fixing its limits. The format is built so that a decoder written to the rules reads every file that follows the rules.

sections.title: Pixels, Colour and Transparency
sections.content:
Conceptually a PNG image is a rectangular array of pixels, left to right within each scanline and top to bottom. The bit depth gives the number of bits per sample in the image data, and three kinds of pixel are supported: an indexed-color pixel that is an index into a supplied palette, a grayscale pixel that is a single luminance level, and a truecolor pixel made of red, green and blue samples. Optionally, grayscale and truecolor pixels can also carry an alpha sample.

All integers of more than one byte are in network byte order, the most significant byte first, and values are unsigned unless noted. Colour values run from zero for black to the maximum value for the sample depth, which is (2^sampledepth)-1 rather than 2^sampledepth. Source data at a precision PNG does not support, such as 5 bit per sample truecolor, must be scaled up to the next higher supported bit depth; the scaling is reversible and loses nothing.

Pixels are packed into scanlines with no wasted bits between them, and a pixel smaller than a byte never crosses a byte boundary. Scanlines always begin on byte boundaries, and one extra filter type byte is placed in front of every scanline. That byte is not part of the image data, but it does go into the compressed stream.

The alpha channel says how opaque each pixel is. A value of zero means fully transparent and the maximum value for the bit depth means fully opaque, with values in between partly transparent. Alpha can only be used with 8 or 16 bit samples, and the alpha sample is stored directly after the colour samples of its pixel. The colour values are not changed by the alpha value, which the RFC calls unassociated or non-premultiplied alpha. Transparency can also be expressed without a full alpha channel through the tRNS chunk. With neither an alpha channel nor a tRNS chunk, every pixel is fully opaque.

For progressive display an image can be stored interlaced. Interlace method 1, named Adam7 after its author Adam M. Costello, splits the image into seven passes over a repeating 8 by 8 pattern, each pass carrying a subset of the pixels. Interlacing slightly expands the file size on average, but it gives a meaningful display much more quickly, and decoders are required to be able to read interlaced images whether or not they perform progressive display.
sections.plainLanguage: A PNG image is a grid of pixels. Each pixel holds a shade of gray, or red, green and blue values, or an index into a colour table. An optional extra value per pixel says how see-through it is. The RFC also describes an interlaced layout that sends the image in seven passes so a viewer can show something early.

sections.title: File Structure and Chunk Names
sections.content:
A PNG file is a PNG signature followed by a series of chunks. The signature is the first eight bytes of the file, always the same decimal values: 137 80 78 71 13 10 26 10. It tells a reader that the rest of the file holds a single PNG image, made of chunks that begin with an IHDR chunk and end with an IEND chunk.

Each chunk has four parts. The Length is a 4-byte unsigned integer giving the number of bytes in the chunk's data field; it counts only the data, not the length itself, the type code or the CRC, zero is a valid length, and it must not exceed (2^31)-1 bytes. The Chunk Type is a 4-byte type code, restricted to the ASCII letters A-Z and a-z, though encoders and decoders must treat the codes as fixed binary values rather than character strings. The Chunk Data holds whatever the type calls for and may be empty. The CRC is a 4-byte cyclic redundancy check over the type code and the data, and it is always present even for a chunk with no data.

Chunk type codes are assigned so that a decoder can tell some things about a chunk even when it does not recognise the type. Bit 5 of each byte carries a property, and the case of each letter shows it to a human reader. The ancillary bit in the first byte marks a chunk that is not strictly needed to display the image, so an unknown ancillary chunk can be ignored safely; the same bit cleared marks a critical chunk, which a decoder that does not understand must report. The private bit in the second byte separates registered public chunks from private ones, so that the two cannot collide. The reserved bit in the third byte must be zero in a conforming file. The safe-to-copy bit in the fourth byte tells editors whether an unrecognised chunk may be copied into a modified file: if the chunk depends on the image data, it must be dropped when critical chunks change.

Chunk CRCs use the standard CRC methods with pre and post conditioning defined by ISO 3309 or ITU-T V.42. The 32-bit register starts as all ones, each byte is processed from its least significant bit to its most significant bit, and the register is inverted at the end and stored most significant byte first.
sections.plainLanguage: Every PNG file starts with eight fixed bytes that identify it, then a list of chunks. A chunk says how long its data is, what kind of chunk it is, the data itself, and a check number computed over the type and the data. The letters in the chunk name carry flags that tell a program whether it may skip the chunk.

sections.title: Chunk Types and Their Order
sections.content:
All implementations must understand the critical chunks, and a valid PNG image must contain an IHDR chunk, one or more IDAT chunks and an IEND chunk. The IHDR image header must appear first. It holds the width and height as 4-byte integers where zero is invalid and the maximum is (2^31)-1, the bit depth, the colour type, the compression method, the filter method and the interlace method, each of the last five as a single byte. The bit depth is the number of bits per sample or per palette index and its valid values are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. The colour type is a sum of 1 for a palette, 2 for colour and 4 for an alpha channel, so the valid values are 0, 2, 3, 4 and 6, and the allowed bit depths differ for each colour type.

The PLTE palette chunk holds from 1 to 256 entries of three bytes each, red, green and blue. It is required for colour type 3, optional for colour types 2 and 6 where it gives a suggested palette, and must not appear for colour types 0 and 4. A chunk length that is not divisible by 3 is an error, and there must not be more than one PLTE chunk. The IDAT chunk holds the compressed image data, produced by laying out the scanlines, filtering them and compressing the result. There can be several IDAT chunks but they must be consecutive, and their boundaries have no meaning: the compressed datastream is simply the concatenation of their contents. The IEND trailer must appear last, marks the end of the datastream and has an empty data field.

The ancillary chunks are optional and hold background colour (bKGD), chromaticities (cHRM), gamma (gAMA), a palette histogram (hIST), physical pixel dimensions (pHYs), significant bits (sBIT), text (tEXt and zTXt), a modification time (tIME) and simple transparency (tRNS).

Because new chunk types will be added over time, the RFC sets rules for how chunks are ordered and how an editor that modifies a file must treat chunks it does not recognise. An editor must not move an unknown unsafe-to-copy chunk relative to a critical chunk, must not move an unknown safe-to-copy chunk from before IDAT to after IDAT or the other way round, and must give up on an unknown critical chunk rather than process the file. An ancillary chunk type may have ordering requirements relative to critical chunks if it is unsafe to copy, or relative to IDAT if it is safe to copy, and no stricter rule is allowed. Critical chunks may have arbitrary ordering requirements, which is why IHDR is allowed the rule that it always appears first.
sections.plainLanguage: Three chunks are essential: a header that describes the image, one or more chunks of compressed picture data, and a trailer that marks the end. Other chunks are optional extras. The RFC also tells programs that edit PNG files how to move chunks around safely when they do not recognise one.

sections.title: Compression and Filtering
sections.content:
PNG compression method 0, the only method defined, is deflate and inflate compression with a 32K sliding window. Deflate is an LZ77 derivative used by zip, gzip and pkzip, and the RFC notes that extensive research supports its patent-free status. The compressed data inside PNG is stored in the zlib format, which the RFC describes as a compression method and flags byte, an additional flags and check bits byte, the compressed data blocks and a 4-byte check value computed on the uncompressed data. For PNG the zlib method code must be 8, meaning deflate, with an LZ77 window of no more than 32K, and a preset dictionary must not be specified. The concatenation of the contents of all the IDAT chunks makes up one zlib datastream, and the boundaries between IDAT chunks can fall anywhere in it, even splitting the terminating check value.

Before compression the image data is filtered. Filtering does not reduce the size of the data itself, but it improves how well the data compresses, and all PNG filters are strictly lossless. PNG defines five filter types, named None, Sub, Up, Average and Paeth, and the encoder may choose a different one for each scanline. In the stream sent to the compression step, each scanline is preceded by a filter type byte saying which filter was used.

The filters work on bytes rather than on pixels, whatever the bit depth or colour type, and alpha data is filtered the same way as image data. For an interlaced image each pass is treated as an independent image, and the previous scanline is the one previously transmitted in the same pass. The bytes to the left of the first pixel in a scanline are treated as zero, and for the first scanline of an image or pass the whole prior scanline is treated as zeroes. Each filter predicts a byte from its neighbours and sends the difference, which is what makes the data compress better; the decoder reverses the prediction. Because the filters refer to the prior scanline, a decoder must keep at least one scanline of image data at all times.
sections.plainLanguage: The picture data is squeezed twice. First each row of pixels is rewritten as differences from neighbouring pixels, which often makes similar numbers sit next to each other. Then the whole thing is compressed with the same deflate algorithm that zip files use. Both steps can be undone exactly, so the picture never changes.

sections.title: Error Checking and Security
sections.content:
A PNG file is a collection of explicitly typed chunks, and a chunk whose contents the specification defines could in fact contain anything, including malicious code. The RFC states that there is no known risk that such code could be executed on the recipient's computer as a result of decoding the PNG image. Unknown or unimplemented chunk types add no further risk, because such chunks are ignored or at most copied into another PNG file.

The text chunks tEXt and zTXt hold data meant to be shown as plain text. If a decoder displays that text without filtering out control characters, especially the escape character, some systems or terminals could behave in undesirable and insecure ways, so the RFC recommends that decoders filter out control characters.

Because every chunk states its length at the beginning and every chunk ends with a CRC, there is a robust defence against corrupted data and against fraudulent chunks that try to overflow a decoder's buffers. The signature bytes also give early detection of common transmission errors. A decoder that does not check CRCs can be subject to data corruption, the likely consequence being wrongly displayed pixels, and a worse case is a corrupted width or height field in IHDR. A poorly written decoder might be subject to buffer overflow, because chunks can be as large as (2^31)-1 bytes, though properly written decoders handle large chunks without difficulty.

The decoder recommendations follow this line of thought. Decoders should verify all eight bytes of the signature, may gain confidence by checking that the next eight bytes are an IHDR chunk header with the correct length, and are strongly recommended to verify the CRC on each chunk. An unknown chunk type is not an error unless it is a critical chunk. An unexpected chunk length in a known chunk such as IHDR is an error, and an unexpected value in a field is treated as fatal only in a critical chunk, since an unexpected value in an ancillary chunk can be handled by ignoring that chunk.
sections.plainLanguage: Each chunk carries its length and a check number, so a damaged file is usually caught quickly and cannot easily be used to overfill a program's memory. The RFC warns programs that show text from a PNG file to strip out control characters first, because a terminal can react badly to them.

viz.caption: THE IHDR IMAGE HEADER AS LAID OUT IN THE RFC

fields.name: Width
fields.desc: Image width in pixels, as a 4-byte integer. Zero is invalid and the maximum is (2^31)-1.

fields.name: Height
fields.desc: Image height in pixels, as a 4-byte integer. Zero is invalid and the maximum is (2^31)-1.

fields.name: Bit depth
fields.desc: Bits per sample or per palette index. Valid values are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16.

fields.name: Colour type
fields.desc: How to read the samples. Valid values are 0, 2, 3, 4 and 6.

fields.name: Compression method
fields.desc: Only 0 is defined: deflate/inflate compression with a 32K sliding window.

fields.name: Filter method
fields.desc: Only 0 is defined: adaptive filtering with five filter types.

fields.name: Interlace method
fields.desc: 0 for no interlace, 1 for Adam7 interlace.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PROPERTY BITS IN A CHUNK TYPE CODE

items.title: Ancillary bit
items.text: Bit 5 of the first byte. Zero means critical and one means ancillary. An unknown ancillary chunk can be ignored safely.

items.title: Private bit
items.text: Bit 5 of the second byte. Zero means public and one means private, so a private chunk name has a lowercase second letter.

items.title: Reserved bit
items.text: Bit 5 of the third byte. It must be zero in a file that conforms to version 1.0, so the third letter is always uppercase.

items.title: Safe-to-copy bit
items.text: Bit 5 of the fourth byte. One means an editor may copy an unrecognised chunk even when it has changed the image data.

items.label: Sub
items.desc: Sends the difference between each byte and the byte of the prior pixel.

items.label: Up
items.desc: Sends the difference between each byte and the byte of the pixel above.

items.label: Average
items.desc: Predicts each byte from the average of the pixel to the left and the pixel above.

items.label: Paeth
items.desc: Predicts each byte from whichever of the left, above and upper-left pixels is closest to a linear estimate.
